activities.caption: bet on the handover before you read on
activities.name: abFizzPredict

config.q: Vinegar stings, soap feels slippery, and baking soda fizzes in vinegar. What is being handed over in every acid–base reaction?
choices: Protons (H⁺ ions) — from acid to base
Oxygen atoms — from base to acid
config.why: An acid is a proton donor and a base a proton acceptor (Brønsted and Lowry, 1923) — nearly every sharp taste and slick feel is that handover happening on your tongue or skin.

activities.anchor: Read the curve from right to left
activities.caption: call the log ruler's jump
activities.name: abLemonEstimate

config.prompt: Lemon juice sits at pH 2, neutral water at pH 7. Roughly how many times more H⁺ does the lemon juice hold?
config.why: About 100,000 times — each single step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, and five steps down the scale is 10⁵.
config.context: That compression is how fourteen powers of ten fit on one 0–14 ruler.

activities.caption: true or false — the alkaline-diet claim
activities.name: abBufferJudge

statements.s: Eating alkaline foods shifts your blood pH and prevents disease.
statements.why: The bicarbonate buffer, the lungs exhaling CO₂ and the kidneys excreting the excess hold arterial blood between 7.35 and 7.45 regardless of diet.

statements.s: Food can change the pH of urine — which is the system working.
statements.why: Acid-forming diets impose a small excretory load, not a blood-pH shift.

statements.s: Drifting 0.4 beyond the 7.35–7.45 band is life-threatening.
statements.why: Which is why blood carries buffers that soak up small additions of acid or base.

statements.s: A tomato can outvote the buffer arithmetic.
statements.why: It cannot — the claim that diet alkalinises the blood fails against the buffer arithmetic.

activities.anchor: Two words beginners must prise apart
activities.caption: file each fact — strength or concentration
activities.name: abStrengthBuckets

config.prompt: Strong is not concentrated. File each fact:

items.label: the fraction of molecules that actually donate a proton
HCl: essentially every molecule ionises in water
a bottle of it can be very dilute
acetic acid: only about 1 in 100 molecules donates at any moment

config.why: A dilute strong acid can out-acid a concentrated weak one — and safety rules treat them differently.

activities.caption: one line of the neutralisation summary is wrong
activities.name: abNeutralSpot

config.prompt: One line of this neutralisation summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Strong acid + strong base at 25 °C ends at pH 7
Weak acid + strong base leaves a salt slightly alkaline — sodium ethanoate sits above 7
Strong acid + weak base such as ammonia also lands slightly alkaline
'Neutralised' means the acid and base have finished reacting — not that 7 was reached
config.correction: Strong acid + weak base lands slightly acidic.
config.why: The endpoint's pH depends on which acid met which base — 'neutralised' means the reaction finished, not that the number 7 was reached.

activities.anchor: Burn an element and the product left behind is its
activities.caption: pair each oxide with its character
activities.name: abOxideMatch

config.prompt: What burning leaves behind — pair each oxide family with its character:

pairs.right: basic — react with acids; CaO + H₂O gives limewater
acidic — CO₂ + H₂O makes rain naturally slightly acidic
amphoteric — react with both acids and bases, a handy fingerprint

config.why: The pattern is a trend: across one row of the periodic table, Na₂O → Al₂O₃ → SO₃ runs from basic to amphoteric to strongly acidic.

activities.anchor: The answer depends on one property of the wanted salt
activities.caption: choose the salt route by solubility
activities.name: abSaltBranch

config.root: Acid + base → salt + water works for any pair — the design question is which starting materials and how to purify. Choose each route.

start.text: You want copper sulfate, a soluble salt. Which route?

choices.label: Acid + insoluble base — copper oxide into warm sulfuric acid
choices.feedback: Stir in black copper oxide until no more dissolves, filter off the excess, evaporate until crystals form. Done.

choices.label: Precipitation — mix two soluble solutions
choices.feedback: That route is for insoluble salts; copper sulfate dissolves, so nothing precipitates.

soluble.text: Now you want barium sulfate, which will not dissolve. Which route?

choices.label: Precipitation — barium chloride plus sodium sulfate
choices.feedback: A white precipitate forms as the ions swap partners — filter, wash, dry. Safe enough for a barium meal precisely because it will not dissolve.

choices.label: Acid + insoluble base
choices.feedback: The product would never come out of solution — insoluble salts need the swap trick.

precip.text: Last: a sodium salt, from two colourless solutions with no visible endpoint. Which route?

choices.label: Measured titration — trial run with phenolphthalein first
choices.feedback: Find the neutralisation volume in the trial, then repeat without indicator to make the salt solution. Experimental design in one afternoon.

choices.label: Evaporate and hope
choices.feedback: With no endpoint you cannot know when to stop — the assay needs the burette.

titrate.text: Route chosen by solubility: insoluble base for soluble salts, precipitation for insoluble ones, measured neutralisation for sodium and potassium salts.

wrong1.text: Back to the tree — solubility of the product decides.

wrong2.text: Back to the tree — an insoluble product needs two soluble parents.

wrong3.text: Back to the tree — invisible endpoints demand an indicator.

config.why: All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts dissolve; most carbonates and hydroxides do not — the solubility rules are the map for the whole decision.

activities.anchor: the sea's surface pH has shifted
activities.caption: call the ocean's log-scale shift
activities.name: abOceanEstimate

config.prompt: Since industrialisation the ocean's surface pH has dropped about 0.1 unit (8.2 → 8.1). On the log ruler, roughly what percentage more H⁺ is that?
config.why: About 30 per cent more H⁺ — the added CO₂ dissolves as carbonic acid, making it harder for corals, shellfish and plankton to build calcium-carbonate shells.
config.context: Acid rain tells the same log-scale story on land: pH 5.6 natural rain dipping to 4 is twenty-five times more acidic.
